title: Sleep is practice
hookLine: most adults need roughly seven to nine hours, and no practice replaces it

cards: Here's an honest moment in a course full of practices: breathing, gratitude, walking, the view from above. All good. But if you're sleeping five hours a night, none of it can do what sleep does.
You can't breathe your way out of being exhausted, or gratitude-list your way past it. A tired brain is worse at paying attention, which makes it bad at every practice in this camp.
So today's practice isn't a technique at all. It's the one underneath the others.

teach.b: In 2015, two major sleep organizations in the United States reviewed the research and landed in nearly the same place: most adults need seven hours or more, and the usual range given is seven to nine.
Some people need a little less, some a little more. Next, the trap. It feels as if you adapt to short sleep.

You don't, much. In a 2003 study, people who slept six hours a night for two weeks did as badly on attention tests as people kept awake for a night or two. The striking part: they rated themselves only a little sleepy.
Tired people are poor judges of how tired they are. Then the clock inside. Your body runs on a rhythm of about a day, called circadian, from Latin words meaning about a day.
That clock likes regular hours. Going to bed and waking at roughly the same time, even on weekends, is one of the simplest things sleep scientists recommend. Much older texts treat sleep as a gift.
A Psalm in the Bible says it is vain to rise up early and sit up late, "for so he giveth his beloved sleep."
You don't have to share that faith to hear the point: sleep isn't laziness, and it isn't something you earn after enough work.
It's the ground every other practice stands on. So this one is simple, and oddly hard. Pick a bedtime.

how: Sleep specialists commonly recommend a regular bedtime and wake time, seven or more hours for most adults, and keeping the same schedule on weekends.

games.q: it's your bedtime. the day isn't finished and there's one more episode. what does today's practice say?
o: stay up until everything is done.
games.why: go to bed. the day is never finished, and sleep is the ground the other practices stand on.

practice: Think of when you need to wake tomorrow, and count back seven and a half hours, plus a little extra to fall asleep: that's your bedtime.
Say the time inside, clearly, and picture yourself at that hour tonight, putting things down, lights off. If any part of you argues, one more episode, one more scroll, just notice it.

wordCard.voice: Circadian. The body's roughly day-long clock, which likes regular hours, the ground every other practice stands on. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: about a day. the root of circadian, a word coined in the twentieth century for the body's daily clock.

carryVoice: Your line: go to bed. The day isn't finished, and it never is. See you tomorrow.
